claim: Carvedilol and alprenolol activate β2AR at clinically relevant nanomolar concentrations.
source: Carvedilol and alprenolol activate β2AR, which promote G protein signaling and cAMP/PKA activities without action of G protein receptor kinases (GRKs).
evidence: The abstract states that carvedilol and alprenolol activate β2AR at nanomolar concentrations, which is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Carvedilol and alprenolol promote G protein signaling and cAMP/PKA activities without action of GRKs.
source: Carvedilol and alprenolol activate β2AR, which promote G protein signaling and cAMP/PKA activities without action of G protein receptor kinases (GRKs).
evidence: Supported by western blot data showing PKA phosphorylation but minimal GRK phosphorylation (Figures 1, 2), and by Gsα recruitment assays (Figure 3A).

claim: The cAMP/PKA activities induced by carvedilol and alprenolol are restricted within the immediate vicinity of activated β2AR.
source: The cAMP/PKA activities are restricted within the immediate vicinity of activated β2AR, leading to selectively enhance PKA-dependent phosphorylation and stimulation of endogenous L-type calcium channel (LTCC) but not AMPA receptor in rat hippocampal neurons.
evidence: Demonstrated by β2AR-ICUE3 fusion biosensor detecting local cAMP (Figure 3D-E), and by selective phosphorylation of CaV1.2 but not GluA1 (Figure 4).

claim: Carvedilol and alprenolol selectively enhance PKA-dependent phosphorylation and stimulation of endogenous LTCC but not AMPA receptor in rat hippocampal neurons.
source: The cAMP/PKA activities are restricted within the immediate vicinity of activated β2AR, leading to selectively enhance PKA-dependent phosphorylation and stimulation of endogenous L-type calcium channel (LTCC) but not AMPA receptor in rat hippocampal neurons.
evidence: Shown by western blot analysis of phosphorylation (Figure 4A-B) and single channel recordings (Figure 5).

claim: A mutant β2AR lacking the catecholamine binding pocket is preferentially activated by carvedilol but not isoproterenol.
source: Moreover, we have engineered a mutant β2AR that lacks the catecholamine binding pocket. This mutant is preferentially activated by carvedilol but not the orthosteric agonist isoproterenol.
evidence: Demonstrated by cAMP FRET measurements (Figure 6B) and phosphorylation assays (Figure 6C-D) showing differential responses to ISO vs CAR.

claim: Carvedilol activates the mutant β2AR in mouse hippocampal neurons augmenting LTCC activity through cAMP/PKA signaling.
source: Carvedilol activates the mutant β2AR in mouse hippocampal neurons augmenting LTCC activity through cAMP/PKA signaling.
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging of LTCC phosphorylation (Figure 7A-B) and single channel recordings (Figure 7C-G) in neurons expressing mutant β2AR.

claim: GPCRs often signal through both canonical G proteins and noncanonical G protein-independent signaling via GRKs and β-arrestins.
source: GPCRs often signal not only through canonical G proteins but also through noncanonical G protein-independent signaling, frequently via G protein receptor kinases (GRKs) and β-arrestins (Lefkowitz, 2000; Xiang and Kobilka, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature on GPCR signaling mechanisms.

claim: GPCRs undergo ligand-induced phosphorylation at different sites by either GRKs or second messenger dependent protein kinases such as PKA.
source: One of the universal features of GPCRs is that they undergo ligand-induced phosphorylation at different sites by either GRKs or second messenger dependent protein kinases such as protein kinase A (PKA).
evidence: This is established knowledge about GPCR regulation, supported by citations.

claim: Phosphorylated GPCRs may present distinct structural features that favor receptor binding to different signaling partners.
source: The phosphorylated GPCRs thus may present distinct structural features that favor receptor binding to different signaling partners, engaging distinct downstream signaling cascades (Reiter and Lefkowitz, 2006; Lefkowitz, 2007; Nobles et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on GPCR phosphorylation and signaling.

claim: Some ligands can differentially activate a GPCR via functional selectivity or biased signaling.
source: Some ligands can differentially activate a GPCR via a phenomenon known as functional selectivity or biased signaling (Wisler et al., 2014; Zweemer et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on biased GPCR signaling.

claim: β2AR is involved in memory and learning in the central nervous system and regulation of metabolism and cardiovascular function.
source: For example, stimulation of β2 adrenergic receptor (β2AR), a prototypical GPCR involved in memory and learning in the central nervous system (CNS) and regulation of metabolism and cardiovascular function, promotes phosphorylation by both GRKs and PKA (Najafi et al., 2016; Mammarella et al., 2016; Fu et al., 2017; Matera et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to literature on β2AR functions.

claim: Stimulation of β2AR promotes phosphorylation by both GRKs and PKA.
source: For example, stimulation of β2 adrenergic receptor (β2AR), a prototypical GPCR involved in memory and learning in the central nervous system (CNS) and regulation of metabolism and cardiovascular function, promotes phosphorylation by both GRKs and PKA (Najafi et al., 2016; Mammarella et al., 2016; Fu et al., 2017; Matera et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations and confirmed by experimental data in this study (Figures 1-2).

claim: Spatially segregated subpopulations of β2AR undergo exclusive phosphorylation by GRKs or PKA in a single cell.
source: We have recently identified spatially segregated subpopulations of β2AR undergoing exclusive phosphorylation by GRKs or PKA in a single cell. These findings indicate specific GPCR subpopulation-based signaling branches can co-exist in a single cell (Shen et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: GRK-mediated phosphorylation promotes pro-survival and cell growth signaling via β-arrestin-dependent MAPK/ERK pathways.
source: GRK-mediated phosphorylation promotes pro-survival and cell growth signaling via β-arrestin-dependent mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK/ERK) pathways, prompting the search for biased ligands that preferentially activate β-arrestin pathways (Luttrell et al., 1999; Pierce et al., 2000; Kim et al., 2005; Ren et al., 2005; Zidar et al., 2009; Choi et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to literature on GRK/β-arrestin signaling.

claim: cAMP/PKA-dependent phosphorylation of β2AR controls ion channel activity at the plasma membrane in primary hippocampal neurons.
source: On the other hand, our recent studies show that the cAMP/PKA-dependent phosphorylation of β2AR controls ion channel activity at the plasma membrane in primary hippocampal neurons (Shen et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work and confirmed by data in this study (Figures 4-5).

claim: β-blockers are thought to reduce cAMP signaling by reducing basal activity of βARs or blocking agonist-induced receptor activation.
source: β-blockers are thought to reduce cAMP signaling because they either reduce basal activity of βARs or block agonist-induced receptor activation.
evidence: This represents the traditional understanding of β-blocker function.

claim: β-blockers have utility limited by side effects in both the CNS and peripheral tissues.
source: While β-blockers are successful in clinical therapies of a broad range of diseases, their utility is limited by side effects in both the CNS and peripheral tissues (Bakris, 2009; Gorre and Vandekerckhove, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to clinical literature.

claim: Some β-blockers display partial agonism and can promote receptor-Gs coupling at high concentrations in vitro.
source: Indeed, studies have revealed that some β-blockers display partial agonism and can promote receptor-Gs coupling at high concentrations in vitro (Yao et al., 2009; DeVree et al., 2016; Gregorio et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Some β-blockers display intrinsic properties mimicking sympathetic activation (sympathomimetic β-blockers).
source: Accordingly, some β-blockers display intrinsic properties mimicking sympathetic activation (sympathomimetic β-blockers) (Maack et al., 2000; Brixius et al., 2001; Larochelle et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to clinical literature.

claim: Classic cAMP assays do not show even minimal cAMP signal induced by sympathomimetic β-blockers.
source: The mechanism remains poorly understood because classic cAMP assay do not show even minimal cAMP signal induced by these β-blockers (Maack et al., 2000; Brixius et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations and confirmed by data in this study showing no signal with generic ICUE3 sensor (Figure 3B).

claim: Alprenolol, carvedilol, propranolol and CGP12177 stimulate phosphorylation of β2AR at PKA sites in HEK293 cells.
source: We found that various β-blockers including alprenolol (ALP), carvedilol (CAR), propranolol (PRO) and CGP12177 (177) were able to stimulate phosphorylation of β2AR at PKA sites expressed in HEK293 cells, similar to the βAR agonist isoproterenol (ISO) (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot analysis using phospho-specific antibodies shown in Figure 1A.

claim: ICI118551, timolol and metoprolol do not stimulate phosphorylation of β2AR at PKA sites in HEK293 cells.
source: In contrast, other β-blockers, that is ICI118551 (ICI), timolol (TIM) and metoprolol (MET), were not able to do so (Figure 1A).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Ligand-induced phosphorylation of β2AR is blocked by β2AR-specific antagonist ICI but not β1AR-specific antagonist CGP20712A.
source: The ligand-induced phosphorylation of β2AR was blocked by β2AR-specific antagonist ICI but not β1AR-specific antagonist CGP20712A (CGP) (Figure 1B and C, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot analysis with antagonist pretreatment shown in Figures 1B-C.

claim: Carvedilol and alprenolol promote phosphorylation of β2AR by PKA at nanomolar concentrations.
source: We found that CAR and ALP promoted phosphorylation of β2AR by PKA even at nanomolar concentrations (Figure 2A and B, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B), which was paralleled by concentration-dependent increases in phosphorylation of ERK (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by concentration-response western blot analysis shown in Figures 2A-B.

claim: Carvedilol and alprenolol induce concentration-dependent increases in phosphorylation of ERK.
source: We found that CAR and ALP promoted phosphorylation of β2AR by PKA even at nanomolar concentrations (Figure 2A and B, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B), which was paralleled by concentration-dependent increases in phosphorylation of ERK (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The roles of β2AR and PKA in carvedilol/alprenolol-induced phosphorylation are confirmed by inhibition with ICI and H89, respectively.
source: The roles of β2AR and PKA in this phenomenon were confirmed by inhibition of β2AR with ICI and inhibition of PKA with H89, respectively (Figure 2C and D, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot analysis with inhibitor pretreatment shown in Figures 2C-D.

claim: β-blockers induce minimal increases in phosphorylation of β2AR at GRK sites and only at high concentrations.
source: In contrast, those β-blockers induced at best minimal increases in phosphorylation of β2AR at GRK sites and only at high concentrations, consistent with a previous report (Wisler et al., 2007) (Figure 1A and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot analysis shown in Figure 1A and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Isoproterenol promotes robust increases in both PKA and GRK phosphorylation of β2AR at different concentrations ranging from nanomolar to micromolar.
source: As positive control, the βAR agonist ISO promoted robust increases in both PKA and GRK phosphorylation of the receptors at different concentrations ranging from nanomolar to micromolar (Figures 1 and 2, and Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot analysis shown in multiple figures.

claim: β2AR is a prevalent postsynaptic norepinephrine effector at glutamatergic synapses in the CNS.
source: In the CNS, β2AR emerges as a prevalent postsynaptic norepinephrine effector at glutamatergic synapses (Davare et al., 2001; Joiner et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2010; Qian et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to literature on β2AR function in neurons.

claim: β-blockers carvedilol and alprenolol activate β2AR and promote phosphorylation of the receptor by PKA in hippocampal neurons.
source: Consistent with the data from HEK293 cells, we found β-blockers CAR and ALP activated β2AR and promoted phosphorylation of the receptor by PKA in hippocampal neurons (Figure 2E).
evidence: Demonstrated by confocal imaging of PKA-phosphorylated β2AR in neurons shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Isoproterenol, carvedilol and alprenolol increase PLA signals between β2AR and Gsα, indicating recruitment of Gsα to β2AR.
source: We showed that ISO, CAR and ALP were able to increase the PLA signals between β2AR and Gsα, indicating recruitment of Gsα to β2AR (Figure 3A).
evidence: Demonstrated by proximity ligation assay shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Timolol has no effect on the recruitment of Gsα to β2AR.
source: As control, TIM had no effect on the recruitment of Gsα to β2ARs.
evidence: Demonstrated by proximity ligation assay shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The role of Gs/AC in carvedilol-induced PKA phosphorylation of β2AR is validated by AC-specific inhibition with 2',5'-dideoxyadenosine.
source: The role of Gs/AC in CAR-induced PKA phosphorylation of β2AR was further validated by AC-specific inhibition with 2',5'-dideoxyadenosine (ddA, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot analysis with AC inhibitor shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Isoproterenol promotes cAMP signal in HEK293 cells while all β-blockers fail to do so without PDE inhibition.
source: The full agonist ISO promoted cAMP signal in HEK293 cells while all β-blockers failed to do so (Figure 3B), in agreement with the classic definition of β-blockers.
evidence: Demonstrated by FRET-based cAMP measurements shown in Figure 3B.

claim: When cells are treated with non-selective phosphodiesterase inhibitor IBMX, carvedilol, alprenolol and CGP12177 induce small but significant cAMP signal in HEK293 cells.
source: However, when cells were treated with non-selective phosphodiesterase (PDE) inhibitor IBMX, CAR, ALP and CGP12177 were able to induce small but significant cAMP signal in HEK293 cells (Figure 3C), indicating a role of PDE in suppressing and restricting the distribution of cAMP in the cells.
evidence: Demonstrated by FRET-based cAMP measurements with IBMX shown in Figure 3C.

claim: PDE plays a role in suppressing and restricting the distribution of cAMP in cells.
source: However, when cells were treated with non-selective phosphodiesterase (PDE) inhibitor IBMX, CAR, ALP and CGP12177 were able to induce small but significant cAMP signal in HEK293 cells (Figure 3C), indicating a role of PDE in suppressing and restricting the distribution of cAMP in the cells.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that PDE inhibition reveals cAMP signals that were previously undetectable.

claim: When β2AR is exogenously expressed in HEK293 cells, carvedilol and alprenolol induce cAMP signal even without PDE inhibition.
source: When β2AR was exogenously expressed in HEK293 cells, CAR and ALP were able to induce cAMP signal in HEK293 cells even without PDE inhibition (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), probably due to insufficient cAMP-hydrolytic activity of endogenous PDEs to counter cAMP production induced from overexpressed β2AR.
evidence: Demonstrated by FRET-based cAMP measurements in cells overexpressing β2AR shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Carvedilol and alprenolol promote cAMP signals within the immediate vicinity of activated β2AR even at nanomolar concentrations.
source: CAR and ALP promoted cAMP signals within the immediate vicinity of activated β2AR even at nanomolar concentrations (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: Demonstrated by β2AR-ICUE3 fusion biosensor measurements shown in Figures 3D-E.

claim: Local increases of cAMP induced by carvedilol and alprenolol are abolished by inhibition of β2AR with ICI or inhibition of ACs with ddA.
source: The local increases of cAMP were abolished by inhibition of β2AR with ICI or inhibition of ACs with ddA (Figure 3E).
evidence: Demonstrated by β2AR-ICUE3 fusion biosensor measurements with inhibitors shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Neither CAAX-ICUE3 nor LYN-ICUE3 can sense cAMP induced by carvedilol and alprenolol, while ISO-induced cAMP is readily detectable on plasma membrane.
source: Interestingly, neither CAAX-ICUE3 targeting to the non-rafts regions of PM nor LYN-ICUE3 targeting to the rafts regions of PM could sense cAMP induced by CAR and ALP, while ISO induced cAMP were readily detectable on PM (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), this further demonstrates that CAR and ALP only promote cAMP within the immediate vicinity of β2AR.
evidence: Demonstrated by FRET measurements with membrane-targeted biosensors shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Carvedilol and alprenolol, but not timolol, significantly increase PKA phosphorylation of S1928 and S1700 of CaV1.2 in hippocampal neurons.
source: CAR and ALP, but not TIM significantly increased PKA phosphorylation of S1928 and S1700 of central α11.2 subunit of CaV1.2 in hippocampal neurons when both β2AR and LTCC were endogenously expressed (Figure 4A, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot analysis of LTCC phosphorylation shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Carvedilol and alprenolol fail to promote phosphorylation of AMPAR subunit GluA1 on its PKA site serine 845.
source: However, CAR and ALP failed to promote phosphorylation of the AMPAR subunit GluA1 on its PKA site serine 845 (Figure 4B, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot analysis of GluA1 phosphorylation shown in Figure 4B.

claim: CaV1.2 and AMPARs are associated with β2AR in hippocampal neurons.
source: Like CaV1.2, AMPARs are associated with β2AR, Gs, AC and PKA (Davare et al., 2001; Joiner et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2010; Qian et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on receptor-channel complexes.

claim: Carvedilol and alprenolol-induced PKA phosphorylation of LTCC is blocked by β2AR inhibitor ICI, AC inhibitor ddA, and PKA inhibitor H89, but not CaMKII inhibitor KN93.
source: Meanwhile, the CAR and ALP-induced PKA phosphorylation of LTCC were blocked by β2AR inhibitor ICI, AC inhibitor ddA, and PKA inhibitor H89, but not CaMKII inhibitor KN93, validating the activation of β2AR-cAMP-PKA pathway (Figure 4C, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot analysis with various inhibitors shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Carvedilol but not timolol significantly increases the open probability, channel availability and mean ensemble average of endogenous LTCC in rat hippocampal neurons.
source: Consistent with the phosphorylation data, CAR but not TIM significantly increased the open probability, channel availability and mean ensemble average of endogenous LTCC in rat hippocampal neurons (Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by cell-attached single channel recordings shown in Figure 5.

claim: Carvedilol stimulates LTCC channel activity when present in the patch pipette solution but not when applied outside the patch via bath perfusion.
source: CAR stimulated channel activity when present in the patch pipette solution but not when applied outside the patch via bath perfusion (Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Demonstrated by single channel recordings with different drug application methods shown in Figure 5.

claim: In backfilling experiments with carvedilol, L-type channel activity is relatively low at the beginning of the recording but significantly increases as the drug diffuses to the pipette tip.
source: Moreover, backfilling experiments with CAR found that L-type channels activity was relatively low at the beginning of the recording but then it significantly increased as the drug diffused to the pipette tip (Figure 5F–G and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Demonstrated by time-course single channel recordings with backfilled pipettes shown in Figures 5F-G.

claim: Isoproterenol applied outside the patch via bath perfusion is able to stimulate LTCC activity.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis and prior studies (Davare et al., 2001), ISO applied outside the patch via bath perfusion was still able to stimulate LTCC activity (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by single channel recordings with bath-applied ISO shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Activation of LTCC by carvedilol promotes cell death in cortical neuron cultures.
source: We further found that the activation of LTCC by CAR promoted cell death in cortical neuron cultures, and inhibition of β2AR or LTCC counteracted carvedilol-induced neuronal toxicities (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by MTT cell viability assay shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Inhibition of β2AR or LTCC counteracts carvedilol-induced neuronal toxicities.
source: We further found that the activation of LTCC by CAR promoted cell death in cortical neuron cultures, and inhibition of β2AR or LTCC counteracted carvedilol-induced neuronal toxicities (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by MTT cell viability assay with antagonists shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Mutation of Ser204 and Ser207 sites within β2AR binding pocket abolishes receptor hydrogen bonds with the catecholamine phenoxy moieties.
source: We hypothesized that mutation of Ser204 and Ser207 sites within β2AR binding pocket would abolish receptor hydrogen bonds with the catecholamine phenoxy moieties, thus reducing binding affinity to agonist ISO while having no effect on β-blocker binding (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on structural knowledge of β2AR binding pocket, supported by previous mutagenesis studies cited in the text.

claim: The mutant S204A/S207A β2AR induces a moderate cAMP signal at high but not low concentrations of isoproterenol.
source: The mutant S204A/S207A β2AR induced a moderate cAMP signal at high but not low concentrations of ISO (Figure 6B).
evidence: Demonstrated by FRET-based cAMP measurements shown in Figure 6B.

claim: After stimulation with carvedilol, the β2AR mutant S204A/S207A promotes significant cAMP signals at nanomolar concentrations with a concentration response curve similar to wild-type β2AR.
source: In contrast, after stimulation with CAR, the β2AR mutant S204A/S207A promoted significant cAMP signals at nanomolar concentrations; the overall concentration response curve was similar to those induced by WT β2AR (Figure 6B).
evidence: Demonstrated by FRET-based cAMP measurements shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Isoproterenol-induced PKA phosphorylation of β2AR S204A/S207A mutant is selectively abolished at nanomolar concentrations.
source: Accordingly, the ISO-induced PKA phosphorylation of β2AR S204A/S207A mutant was selectively abolished at nanomolar concentrations. At higher concentrations, ISO was able to induce reduced PKA phosphorylation of the β2AR S204A/S207A mutant when compared to WT β2AR, consistent with the data of cAMP signals (Figure 6C, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Isoproterenol fails to induce GRK phosphorylation of β2AR S204A/S207A mutant at different concentrations.
source: Meanwhile, ISO failed to induce GRK phosphorylation of β2AR S204A/S207A mutant at different concentrations (Figure 6C).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Carvedilol induces equivalent PKA phosphorylation of β2AR wild-type and S204A/S207A mutant at different concentrations.
source: In comparison, CAR induced equivalent PKA phosphorylation of β2AR WT and S204A/S207A mutant at different concentrations (Figure 6D, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: In DKO neurons expressing the mutant S204A/S207A β2AR, carvedilol but not isoproterenol (30 nM) promotes PKA phosphorylation of LTCC α11.2.
source: In DKO neurons expressing the mutant S204A/S207A β2AR, CAR, but not ISO (30 nM) promoted PKA phosphorylation of LTCC α11.2 (Figure 7A and B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by confocal imaging of LTCC phosphorylation shown in Figures 7A-B.

claim: In DKO neurons expressing mutant S204A/S207A β2AR, carvedilol but not isoproterenol significantly increases the open probability, channel availability and mean ensemble average of LTCC.
source: In agreement, CAR, but not ISO significantly increased the open probability, channel availability and mean ensemble average of LTCC (Figure 7C–7G).
evidence: Demonstrated by single channel recordings shown in Figures 7C-G.

claim: Carvedilol and alprenolol are Gs-biased partial agonists of βAR for highly spatially restricted cAMP/PKA signaling to CaV1.2 in neurons.
source: Our study defines CAR and ALP as Gs-biased partial agonists of βAR for highly spatially restricted cAMP/PKA signaling to CaV1.2 in neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing selective Gs/PKA activation without GRK activation and restricted cAMP signaling.

claim: PKA-mediated phosphorylation plays critical roles in heterologous desensitization of GPCRs and in receptor switching from Gs to Gi coupling.
source: PKA-mediated phosphorylation is thought to play critical roles in heterologous desensitization of GPCRs and in receptor switching from Gs to Gi coupling (Daaka et al., 1997; Zamah et al., 2002), whereas GRK-mediated phosphorylation is implicated in β-arrestin recruitment and β-arrestin-dependent ERK activation (Luttrell et al., 1999; Pierce et al., 2000; Kim et al., 2005; Ren et al., 2005; Zidar et al., 2009; Choi et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on GPCR phosphorylation and regulation.

claim: GRK-mediated phosphorylation is implicated in β-arrestin recruitment and β-arrestin-dependent ERK activation.
source: PKA-mediated phosphorylation is thought to play critical roles in heterologous desensitization of GPCRs and in receptor switching from Gs to Gi coupling (Daaka et al., 1997; Zamah et al., 2002), whereas GRK-mediated phosphorylation is implicated in β-arrestin recruitment and β-arrestin-dependent ERK activation (Luttrell et al., 1999; Pierce et al., 2000; Kim et al., 2005; Ren et al., 2005; Zidar et al., 2009; Choi et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on GRK/β-arrestin signaling.

claim: PKA and GRKs phosphorylate distinct subpopulations of β2AR in a single fibroblast or neuron.
source: We have recently characterized that PKA and GRKs phosphorylate distinct subpopulations of β2AR in a single fibroblast or neuron (Shen et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: While GRK phosphorylation of β2AR is only observed at high concentrations of agonists, PKA phosphorylation can be induced with minimal doses of agonist.
source: While GRK phosphorylation of β2AR is only observed at high concentrations of agonists, PKA phosphorylation can be induced with minimal doses of agonist (Shen et al., 2018; Tran et al., 2004; Tran et al., 2007; Liu et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies and confirmed by data in this study.

claim: Carvedilol does not promote GRK phosphorylation at low concentrations and induces a slow and minimal GRK effect at high concentrations when compared to isoproterenol.
source: Here, our data show CAR does not promote GRK phosphorylation at low concentrations and induces a slow and minimal GRK effect at high concentrations when compared to those induced by ISO.
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot analysis shown in Figures 1-2 and supplementary figures.

claim: Carvedilol has been recognized as a biased β-blocker that preferentially activates β-arrestin/ERK pathways.
source: Previously, CAR has been recognized as a biased β-blocker that preferentially activates β-arrestin/ERK pathways (Wisler et al., 2007; Kim et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: GRK phosphorylation of β2AR is not necessary for carvedilol-induced activation of ERK.
source: Despite the prominent role of GRK phosphorylation in full agonist ISO-induced β2AR-β-arrestin/ERK signaling, our data clearly indicate that GRK phosphorylation of β2AR is not necessary for CAR-induced activation of ERK, consistent with a recent study showing a distinct general mechanism of β-arrestin activation that does not require the GRK-phosphorylated tail of different GPCRs (Eichel et al., 2018).
evidence: Inferred from data showing ERK activation without GRK phosphorylation, supported by citation to recent literature.

claim: In the absence of all G proteins, GPCRs fail to transduce β-arrestin/ERK signaling.
source: Meanwhile, other studies show that in the absence of all G proteins, GPCRs fail to transduce β-arrestin/ERK signaling (Grundmann et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature.

claim: There is a concentration-dependent correlation between PKA phosphorylation of β2AR and ERK activity induced by β-blockers.
source: In our study, we observed a concentration-dependent correlation between PKA phosphorylation of β2AR with ERK activity induced by β-blockers, suggesting the potential role of Gs and PKA in CAR-induced β2AR-β-arrestin/ERK signaling are overlooked.
evidence: Observed from data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Gi is not required for carvedilol-induced β2AR/β-arrestin signaling.
source: In comparison, Gi is not required for CAR-induced β2AR/β-arrestin signaling even though CAR induces Gi recruitment to β1AR for transducing β1AR/β-arrestin signaling (Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation and data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 showing no effect of pertussis toxin.

claim: Activation of β2AR with femtomolar concentrations of ligands causes sustained ERK signaling.
source: Moreover, our results are also in line with a recent report that activation of β2AR with as low as femtomolar concentrations of ligands causes sustained ERK signaling (Civciristov et al., 2018), further support a PKA but GRK-dependent mechanism in GPCR-induced ERK activation.
evidence: Supported by citation to recent literature.

claim: β2AR with S204/207A mutation loses binding to adrenaline but still binds with several β-blockers including alprenolol.
source: Previous mutagenesis studies have shown that β2AR with S204/207A mutation loses binding to adrenaline but still binds with several β-blockers including ALP (Liapakis et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous mutagenesis study.

claim: The S204/207A mutant β2AR is not only refractory to its agonists but also completely lost both ISO- and CAR-induced GRK-phosphorylation of β2AR.
source: Interestingly, the S204/207A β2AR mutant is not only refractory to its agonists but also completely lost both ISO- and CAR-induced GRK-phosphorylation of β2AR.
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot analysis shown in Figure 6C-D.

claim: Many β-blockers possess intrinsic sympathomimetic activities.
source: Many β-blockers possess intrinsic sympathomimetic activities (Bakris, 2009; Gorre and Vandekerckhove, 2010), which are problematic due to the side effects through stimulation of βARs (Bakris, 2009; Gorre and Vandekerckhove, 2010), a feature that limits the clinical utility of the drugs.
evidence: Supported by citations to clinical literature.

claim: β-blockers promote activation of β2AR by recruiting Gs that selectively transduces cAMP/PKA signal but not GRK signal.
source: Here, we show that β-blockers promote activation of β2AR by recruiting Gs that selectively transduces cAMP/PKA signal but not GRK signal.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented throughout the study.

claim: Binding of β-blockers to β1AR enhances cAMP levels locally by dissociating a β1AR-PDE4 complex, thereby reducing the local cAMP-hydrolytic activity.
source: Meanwhile, binding of β-blockers to β1AR has been shown to enhance cAMP levels locally by dissociating a β1AR-PDE4 complex, thereby reducing the local cAMP-hydrolytic activity (Richter et al., 2013), β1AR and β2AR thus could utilize different mechanisms for β-blocker-induced signaling.
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on β1AR-PDE4 interactions.

claim: β1AR and β2AR could utilize different mechanisms for β-blocker-induced signaling.
source: Meanwhile, binding of β-blockers to β1AR has been shown to enhance cAMP levels locally by dissociating a β1AR-PDE4 complex, thereby reducing the local cAMP-hydrolytic activity (Richter et al., 2013), β1AR and β2AR thus could utilize different mechanisms for β-blocker-induced signaling.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of β1AR and β2AR mechanisms described in the text.

claim: The β-blocker-induced β2AR-cAMP signal is sufficient to promote PKA phosphorylation of both β2AR and the receptor-associated CaV1.2 of LTCC, but not AMPAR GluA1 subunit.
source: Another interesting observation is that the β-blocker-induced β2AR-cAMP signal is sufficient to promote PKA phosphorylation of both β2AR and the receptor-associated CaV1.2 of LTCC, but not another substrate, the AMPAR GluA1 subunit.
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Both LTCC and AMPAR are shown to associate with β2AR in hippocampal neurons.
source: Both LTCC and AMPAR are shown to associate with the β2AR in hippocampal neurons (Davare et al., 2001; Joiner et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2010; Qian et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on receptor-channel complexes.

claim: The preference of one local membrane target over another local target indicates a highly restricted nature of the cAMP-PKA activities.
source: Therefore, the preference of one local membrane target over another local target indicates a highly restricted nature of the cAMP-PKA activities, potentially dependent on the recently identified distinct subpopulations of β2AR and associated signaling molecules in the neurons (Shen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the selective phosphorylation data, supported by citation to previous work.

claim: PKA phosphorylation of LTCC leads to augmentation of LTCC activity, potentially contributing to neuronal toxicities.
source: Nevertheless, the PKA phosphorylation leads to augmentation of LTCC activity, potentially contributing to the neuronal toxicities.
evidence: Inferred from data showing increased LTCC activity (Figure 5) and cell death (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).

claim: Activation of GPCR at low ligand concentrations should be taken into consideration when designing and screening new therapeutic drugs.
source: Therefore, activation of GPCR at low ligand concentrations should be taken into consideration when designing and screening new therapeutic drugs.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the findings of the study showing β-blocker activation of β2AR at nanomolar concentrations.

claim: Isoproterenol stimulates LTCC activity in hippocampal neurons.
source: As shown before, ISO stimulates LTCC activity (Figure 5) (Shen et al., 2018; Davare et al., 2001).
evidence: Demonstrated by single channel recordings shown in Figure 5 and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: β2AR functionally interacts with AMPA receptor and L-type Ca2+ channel CaV1.2 at glutamatergic synapses.
source: In the CNS, β2AR emerges as a prevalent postsynaptic norepinephrine effector at glutamatergic synapses, where β2AR functionally interacts with AMPA receptor (AMPAR) and L-type Ca2+ channel (LTCC) CaV1.2, and regulates neuronal excitability and synaptic plasticity (Davare et al., 2001; Joiner et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2010; Qian et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on β2AR function in neurons.

claim: β2AR regulates neuronal excitability and synaptic plasticity.
source: In the CNS, β2AR emerges as a prevalent postsynaptic norepinephrine effector at glutamatergic synapses, where β2AR functionally interacts with AMPA receptor (AMPAR) and L-type Ca2+ channel (LTCC) CaV1.2, and regulates neuronal excitability and synaptic plasticity (Davare et al., 2001; Joiner et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2010; Qian et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on β2AR function in neurons.

claim: Carvedilol and alprenolol promote phosphorylation of β2AR by PKA in hippocampal neurons with similar distribution to agonist-stimulated neurons.
source: Confocal images show PKA-phosphorylated β2AR in agonist- or β-blocker-stimulated neurons have similar distribution. Scale bar, 10 μm. Representative of 6 images for each condition, three experiments.
evidence: Shown by confocal imaging in Figure 2E demonstrating similar subcellular distribution patterns.

claim: Carvedilol and alprenolol are partial agonists of β2AR at clinically relevant concentrations rather than strict antagonists.
source: In this study, using a combination of highly sensitive tools such as engineered FRET-based cAMP sensors and single channel recording together with detection by phospho-specific antibodies, we show for the first time that β-blockers such as CAR and ALP can promote receptor-Gs coupling at nanomolar concentrations in living cells, which is clinically relevant in contrast to superphysiological concentrations in previous studies.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing β2AR activation at nanomolar concentrations.

claim: The differential signaling by carvedilol with respect to LTCC and AMPAR indicates both channels form complexes with β2AR localized within dendritic spines.
source: The differential signaling by carvedilol with respect to LTCC and AMPAR is especially remarkable because both channels form complexes with β2AR that are localized within dendritic spines.
evidence: This is stated as a known fact about the localization of these receptor-channel complexes.

claim: Local cAMP signals possess the potential to selectively regulate downstream effectors in receptor complexes or within the vicinity of activated receptors.
source: Local cAMP signals possess the potential to selectively regulate downstream effectors in receptor complexes or within the vicinity of activated receptors.
evidence: This is a general principle supported by the experimental data showing selective phosphorylation of CaV1.2 but not GluA1.

claim: About 30% of patches show L-type channel activity in hippocampal neurons without BayK in the recording pipette.
source: Diagram reflecting our patch statistics without using BayK in the recording pipette. Only about 30% of our patches showed channel activity.
evidence: Shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A as a pie chart of patch statistics.

claim: Isoproterenol and carvedilol have similar effects on LTCC channel activity whether BayK is included or not in the pipette solution.
source: Note that ISO and CAR had similar effects on channel activity whether BayK was included or not in the pipette solution.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the electrophysiology experiments.

claim: BayK-8644 promotes longer open times of L-type Ca2+ channels and helps resolve channel openings.
source: This pipette solution was supplemented with 1 µM ω-conotoxin GVIA and 1 µM ω-conotoxin MCVIIC to block N and P/Q-type Ca2+ channels, respectively, and (S)-(-)-BayK-8644 (500 nM) was included in the pipette solution to promote longer open times and resolve channel openings as previously performed by our group and others (Shen et al., 2018; Davare et al., 2001; Wang et al., 2001; Qian et al., 2017; Hess et al., 1986; Schuhmann et al., 1997; Costantin et al., 1998; Yue and Marban, 1990; Dzhura and Neely, 2003; Navedo et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a methodological detail supported by citations to previous studies using this approach.
